blocks.x: Introduction:

Dragon fruit, popularly known worldwide as pitaya or strawberry pear, has recently gained attention in India not only for its nutritional value but also for its unique identity. In 2021, the Chief Minister of Gujarat, Vijay Rupani, named this fruit “Kamalam,” inspired by its bright pink color and resemblance to a lotus. Scientifically, dragon fruit belongs to the genus Hylocereus under the family Cactaceae. Centre of origin of this fruit is southern Mexico and parts of Central and South America, dragon fruit later spread to Southeast Asia, where it is now cultivated extensively. Its introduction to Asian countries dates back to the 19th century, when European missionaries brought it to the region. Over time, countries like Vietnam, China, Thailand, Malaysia, and Indonesia emerged as major producers, with Vietnam alone contributing a significant share of global production (Merten, 2003). In India, dragon fruit cultivation began in the late 1990s and has since expanded rapidly. States such as Gujarat, Karnataka, and Maharashtra are currently leading producers, while its cultivation has also spread to regions like Himachal Pradesh, Jammu and Kashmir, Rajasthan, and northeastern states such as Tripura, Mizoram, and Nagaland. This wide adaptability highlights its potential as a commercially viable fruit crop across diverse agro-climatic conditions.

Dragon fruit is often regarded as a “super fruit” due to its impressive nutritional composition and health-promoting properties. On a fresh weight basis (100 g), the fruit contains about 80-85% water, making it highly refreshing, along with moderate amounts of natural sugars (4.5-7.5 g) and carbohydrates (10-13 g). It is also a good source of dietary fiber (2.5-3.0%), which supports digestive health. The fruit provides essential vitamins such as vitamin C (4-10 mg), vitamin A (59 IU), riboflavin, niacin, thiamine, and a small amount of vitamin E. In addition, it is rich in important minerals including potassium (270-400 mg), magnesium (27-39 mg), calcium (18 mg), phosphorus (19-36 mg), and iron (0.7-1.0 mg). With an energy value of around 60-66 kcal per 100 g, it offers balanced nutrition without being calorie-dense (Jaafar et al., 2009). A notable feature of dragon fruit is its antioxidant content. The pink-fleshed varieties contain higher levels of phenolic compounds and flavonoids compared to white-fleshed types, contributing to their stronger antioxidant potential. These bioactive compounds play a key role in enhancing immunity and protecting the body against oxidative stress. Regular consumption of dragon fruit is associated with several health benefits. It helps improve digestion due to its fiber content, supports immune function, and may reduce the risk of chronic diseases such as diabetes, cardiovascular disorders, and certain types of cancer. Botanically, dragon fruit is a fast-growing, perennial cactus climber with thick, succulent, green stems that perform the function of leaves. These stems have wavy, ribbed margins with small spines along the edges. At each spine point
(areole), a dormant bud is present, from which flowers and subsequently fruits develop. The plant is classified as a semi-epiphytic or xerophytic species, well adapted to dry conditions.

Globally, countries like Vietnam, China, and Indonesia dominate dragon fruit production, together contributing more than 90% of the total output. Among them, Vietnam is the leading producer, with around 1.4 million tonnes cultivated over 55,000 hectares and productivity ranging between 22-35 tonnes per hectare. A significant portion (about 80%) of its production is exported to China. In India, dragon fruit (locally referred to as Kamalam) is emerging as a promising horticultural crop, currently grown on approximately 14.5 thousand hectares with a production of about 53.7 thousand metric tonnes. Recognizing its economic potential, efforts are underway to expand the cultivation area to nearly 50,000 hectares in the coming years. The fruit enjoys strong demand both domestically and internationally. Major importing markets for Asian dragon fruit include China, Europe, and America, while India has begun exporting to countries such as Qatar, Maldives, and Saudi Arabia. Among exporting nations, Vietnam, China, and Ecuador are the leading players in the global dragon fruit trade.

Dragon fruit is well adapted to tropical and sub-tropical climates and can grow under a wide range of environmental conditions, from humid to relatively dry regions. It performs best within an optimal temperature range of about 6-20°C during winter and 25-40°C in summer. The crop can tolerate varying rainfall conditions, from around 500 mm as seen in Baramati to as high as 2500 mm in regions like Tripura. However, it is highly sensitive to waterlogging, and therefore, low-lying areas with poor drainage are not suitable for its cultivation. The plant is delicate in nature and particularly vulnerable to extreme climatic conditions. Exposure to sub-zero or freezing temperatures can cause severe injury, making it unsuitable for temperate regions. On the other hand, prolonged exposure to temperatures above 40°C, along with cloudy weather, high humidity, and continuous heavy rainfall, can adversely affect plant growth, flowering, and fruit development (McMahon, 2003).

Although dragon fruit can grow in a variety of soils, it thrives best in loose, well-drained, fertile soils rich in organic matter, particularly sandy to loamy types. The ideal soil pH ranges between 5.0 and 7.0. Water stagnation near the collar region should be strictly avoided, as it can lead to rotting and abnormal rooting of the fleshy stems, exposing the central rib. The production of healthy and disease-free planting material is crucial for successful cultivation, as it helps prevent the spread of diseases like anthracnose and bacterial spot, as well as pests such as mealybugs and aphids. It is important to source plants from reliable nurseries where mother plants are well-maintained under proper nutrient and plant protection practices (Mallik et al., 2018). Propagation is commonly done through stem cuttings taken from one-year-old plants. Cuttings of about 20- 30 cm length are planted in polybags filled with a mixture of soil, sand, and farmyard manure or vermicompost in a 3:1:1 ratio, or in soilless media like cocopeat. To minimize the risk of soil-borne diseases, the rooting medium is treated with fungicides such as carbendazim and mancozeb or bioagents like Trichoderma. Cuttings are usually collected between June and October and raised under protected conditions such as polyhouses or net houses to shield them from excessive rain and direct sunlight.

The plants generally become ready for field planting within 5-8 months, and the ideal planting time is from July to August. Although grafting on seedlings is possible, rooted cuttings are generally preferred due to their better initial growth. For transportation over long distances, rooted plants are carefully packed using moist materials like moss or newspaper to prevent drying, and then placed in corrugated fiber boxes (To et al., 2002). With the increasing demand for dragon fruit across different regions, the production and sale of quality planting material has become a profitable venture. Nursery growers can earn substantial income by supplying healthy plants, often priced around ₹50-60 per plant, in addition to income from fruit production. Dragon fruit varieties are mainly classified based on the colour of their skin and flesh, which are closely linked to their species. Among the important species, Hylocereus polyrhizus produces fruits with red skin and red flesh, while Hylocereus costaricensis has red skin with attractive purple flesh. Hylocereus undatus is the most common type, characterized by red skin and white flesh, whereas Hylocereus megalanthus bears yellow-skinned fruits with white pulp. Among these, fruits with red or purple flesh are generally more preferred by consumers due to their appealing colour and higher antioxidant content. However, red-skinned fruits with white flesh also enjoy strong market demand, particularly in countries like China. Based on skin and flesh colour, dragon fruit varieties can be broadly grouped into four categories. Red-fleshed types have pink skin with deep red pulp, including popular cultivars such as Costa Rican Sunset, Bloody Mary, Red Jaina, Zamorano, Alice Red, Moroccan Red, Jumbo Red, Vietnam Red, and Natural Mystic (Rahim et al., 2009). Pink or purple-fleshed types have reddish skin with pink to purple pulp, and include varieties like Delight, Dark Star, Purple Haze, Makisupa, Cosmic Charlie, Townsend, and American Beauty. White-fleshed types, which have pink skin and white pulp, include varieties such as David Bowie, LA Woman, Delight, Alice, and Neitzel. Yellow types are distinguished by their yellow skin and white flesh, with examples like Pitaya megalanthus, Israeli Yellow, Colombia Yellow, and Golden Dragon.

Spacing in the main field varies depending on the planting system adopted. Under the square system, spacing of 2 x 2 m or 3 x 3 m is commonly followed. In improved systems such as wire trellis, closer spacing is practiced, with 1-1.5 m between plants and 1.5-2 m between rows, allowing efficient use of space and better canopy management (Patel and Ishnava, 2019).

Dragon fruit is a climbing cactus, it cannot grow upright without support. Therefore, a strong and durable support system is essential for proper growth and yield. Traditionally, concrete poles reinforced with iron rods are used. These poles are typically 6-7 feet tall and 4-6 inches in diameter, with about one foot embedded into the soil and fixed firmly using cement. A circular structure, often made using a discarded tyre supported by iron rods, is placed at the top to allow branches to spread and hang freely. Usually, four plants are planted around each pole at equal distances, though in some cases, two plants are preferred for easier management (Barbeau, 1990 and Le Bellec, 2004). Alternatively, modern support systems such as angle iron poles with T-bar structures are also used. In this system, poles are installed at regular intervals, and galvanized wires are stretched across the top. Individual plants are trained along these wires, allowing the branches to cascade on both sides. This method not only supports the plant effectively but also improves light exposure, air circulation, and ease of harvesting, ultimately contributing to better productivity.
Major diseases of dragon fruit:

In the early stages of its cultivation, dragon fruit was considered relatively free from serious diseases and insect pests. However, with the expansion of its cultivation, several problems have recently emerged, particularly in the northeastern regions of India, posing a challenge to growers. Among the major diseases, Anthracnose caused by Colletotrichum is one of the most damaging. It affects both stems and fruits, and its incidence may vary from 10-60% in the plantations resulting into drying of plants. Another important disease reported in India is stem canker caused by Neoscytalidium dimidiatum. Effective management largely depends on preventive measures such as avoiding excessive pruning and maintaining proper field sanitation, along with timely application of suitable fungicides. Viral infection due to Cactus virus X has also been observed in dragon fruit. Infected plants show symptoms like small dull yellow spots on stems, drying of tissues, and malformed, stunted, and mottled fruits. To minimize the spread of infection, pruning tools should always be sterilized with alcohol or spirit before use, and the cut ends of stems should be protected by applying copper-based fungicidal paste. Other diseases such as stem rot caused by Xanthomonas campestris and fruit brown spot caused by Dothiorella spp. are also reported in dragon fruit plantations. Bacterial spot symptoms may occasionally appear under favorable environmental conditions. Therefore, adopting proper plant protection measures and integrated disease management practices is essential for maintaining healthy and productive dragon fruit orchards.
Anthracnose (Colletotrichum spp.):

Anthracnose caused by Colletotrichum spp. are one of the most devastating preharvest and postharvest diseases of pitaya fruits [Ali et al., 2013; Zahid et al., 2014]. The disease was quite severe in different regions, with about 50% incidence reported in an orchard in Fortaleza in 2018 (Inokuti et al., 2024) and up to 35% in Pelotas in 2017 (Nascimento et al., 2019). In Malaysia, anthracnose led to heavy yield losses ranging from 20% to 80%, and around half of the losses in pitaya were mainly caused by Colletotrichum gloeosporioides (Masyahit et al., 2009). In 2020, the disease was also noticed in greenhouse-grown pitaya (H. undatus) fruits in Wuwei, where about 15.6% of plants were affected (Zahid et al., 2012). However, the pathogens causing anthracnose to differ from one region to another, and detailed identification of these species is still limited worldwide.

blocks.x: The colony of Colletotrichum siamense is characterized by the profuse formation of black acervuli along with pinkish–orange conidial masses. Initially, the mycelium appears white to light grey, but as the colony matures, it gradually turns dark grey from the surface. The acervuli are round to oval in shape, dark brown in colour, and measure approximately 238.05 × 457.49 µm. The setae associated with the acervuli are dark brown to black, rigid and straight, with a swollen base and a tapering pointed tip. The conidia are hyaline (colourless), crescent or sickle-shaped, and measure about 21.27 µm in length and 4.04 µm in width. They possess an acute apex and a narrow, truncate base. Upon germination, each conidium produces a single germ tube, usually emerging from the middle or apical region, which subsequently develops into a spherical to ovate appressorium measuring approximately 8.13 × 11.75 µm (Zhang et al., 2024).
Favorable condition:

Anthracnose of dragon fruit, caused by Colletotrichum species, develops rapidly under warm and humid conditions. High relative humidity (above 85–90%) along with moderate temperatures of about 25–30°C creates an ideal environment for fungal growth, spore germination, and infection. The disease is further favoured by frequent rainfall or overhead irrigation, which helps in the spread of spores through water splash. Prolonged leaf or fruit wetness, usually for 8–12 hours or more, enhances the chances of infection. In addition, poor air circulation, dense planting, and shaded or cloudy conditions maintain moisture on plant surfaces, thereby promoting disease development. Wounds or injuries on fruits also facilitate easy entry of the pathogen, increasing the severity of anthracnose. (Li et al., 2023).
Disease cycle:
Survival and Inoculation

The cycle begins with the fungus surviving as mycelia and conidia within the soil, plant debris, and rotten remains of previously infected dragon fruit. These fungal spores, specifically conidia (asexual spores) and ascospores (sexual spores from the perithecium), serve as the primary inoculum that targets healthy dragon fruit flowers and developing fruits in the field.
Infection and Development

Germination: Once a spore lands on the fruit surface, it germinates by forming a germ tube. Penetration: The fungus moves into the early infection stage, where it develops a specialized structure to penetrate the tough outer skin of the host.
Invasion: Following penetration, the fungus invades the internal host tissues, spreading its hyphae through the cellular layers.
Latency: Interestingly, the disease often enters a latent stage, where the fungus remains dormant and invisible while the fruit is still growing or ripening on the vine.
Symptom Expression and Dissemination:

The most visible damage occurs after harvest, when the fruit tissues begin to collapse, forming characteristic sunken lesions (dark, water-soaked spots). As these symptoms manifest on the dragon fruit surface, the fungus produces acervuli fruiting bodies that erupt to release a new generation of conidia. These spores are then dispersed by wind or rain to infect new crops or return to the soil and debris, effectively completing the disease cycle.
Disease cycle of Anthracnose of Dragon Fruit
Management
Use healthy and disease-free planting material to prevent early infection.

Maintain proper spacing and pruning to improve air circulation and reduce humidity. Avoid overhead irrigation; use drip irrigation to minimize leaf and fruit wetness. Remove and destroy infected fruits, cladodes, and plant debris regularly.
Protect fruits from injury, as wounds help the fungus to enter easily.

Apply preventive sprays of Mancozeb (80% WP) or Bordeaux mixture at regular intervals. Use systemic fungicides like Tebuconazole (25% EC), Difenoconazole (25% EC), or Carbendazim (50% WP) when disease appears.
Spray combination fungicide Carbendazim (12% WP) + Mancozeb (63% WP) for better control. Rotate fungicides to avoid resistance development in the pathogen.
Apply biocontrol agents such as PGPM consortium to reduce disease naturally.
Maintain field sanitation and avoid excess moisture conditions.
Monitor the crop regularly, especially during warm and humid weather, for early detection and timely control. Stem canker (Neoscytalidium dimidiatum)

Dragon fruit has been a relatively low-maintenance crop, but several diseases have arisen with significant impact, likely due to increases in planting acreage and the consequent buildup of pathogen inoculum. Based on a recent survey, stem and fruit canker caused by the fungal pathogen Neoscytalidium dimidiatum is a prevailing disease on dragon fruit in south Florida. The pathogen has also been reported in Southeast Asia, the Middle East, North America, Ecuador, Puerto Rico (South America and Carib bean) and India, causing canker-like symptoms on cladodes (stems) and fruits. (Serrato-Diaz, and Goenaga 2021). In India Stem cankers were seen in commercial orchards in the Satara, Pune, and Solapur districts of Maharashtra. Disease incidence across four orchards was ∼40% and severity was 30 to 80%. Initial symptoms on infected cladodes were minute, circular, depressed chlorotic spots, often with brick red flecks, followed by elevation of the lesion center. Lesions turned necrotic and contained black, erumpent pycnidia, followed by chlorosis and stem rot.
Symptoms:

Stem canker has been widely observed in red-fleshed dragon fruit (Hylocereus polyrhizus) plantations, particularly in Malaysia, and similar trends have also been reported in India. The disease typically begins as small, circular, sunken orange spots on the stems, which later develop black pycnidia and lead to tissue rotting. Field observations indicate that disease incidence can reach around 40%, with severity varying from 30% to 80%. (Sanahuja et al., 2016)

The disease symptoms on cladodes initially appear as small, sunken, chlorotic spots, sometimes with a tiny orange center. As the disease progresses, these spots enlarge and become slightly raised, turning orange to reddish-brown in color. Over time, they may merge to form larger brown lesions. In many cases, the lesions are surrounded by yellow halos or dark brown, water-soaked areas. Small black fruiting bodies (pycnidia) develop within the pale yellow to grey necrotic tissues, which contain large numbers of spores (conidia). These spores spread to nearby healthy tissues and initiate new infections. As the disease advances, the affected areas dry up, leading to perforations in the cladodes, resulting in a characteristic “shot-hole” appearance. The pathogen may also infect fruits, often through the flower tube, causing internal black rot. Since the pathogen can persist in the orchard during the vegetative growth period, it is essential to keep its inoculum level low to reduce damage to stems and fruits. (Salunkhe et al., 2023)

The colony’s white mycelial turned to olive green to grayish with dark gray to black pigmentation. Colony growth was rapid (30 mm/day). Brown, branched septate hyphae fragmented to produce abundant arthroconidia in chains that were hyaline to dark brown, thick walled, 0 to 1 septate, ellipsoid to ovoid (10.1 ± 1.4 × 4.88 ± 1.1 μm), rod (9.0 ± 0.8 μm × 5.3 ± 0.8 μm), round (7.9 ± 1.6 μm) and capsule (14.2 ± 3.1 × 6.1 ± 0.8 μm) shape. Conidia from pycnidia developed on host tissues were aseptate, hyaline and ellipsoid cylindrical (8.2 ± 0.8 × 2.2 ± 0.3 μm) in shape. (Salunkhe et al., 2023)
Favorable condition:

Favorable conditions for stem canker caused by Neoscytalidium dimidiatum are mainly influenced by temperature, moisture, and inoculum level in the orchard. The pathogen shows rapid germination and growth under warm conditions, particularly when temperatures rise from about 22°C to 35°C. Studies indicate that nearly half of the spores can germinate within 24 hours when the temperature exceeds 22°C, which significantly increases disease pressure when inoculum is present in large quantities. Warm and humid environments further promote infection, especially during late spring and the rainy season, when moisture availability supports spore dispersal and infection. Poor sanitation, presence of infected cladodes, and dense canopy conditions also create a favorable microclimate by increasing humidity and reducing airflow. This allows the pathogen to survive, multiply, and spread easily.

Additionally, the disease becomes more severe when young, tender cladodes emerge, as they are highly susceptible to infection. If orchards are not kept clean during cooler and drier periods (such as winter and early spring), the pathogen can persist and build up, making disease management difficult once temperatures increase. Therefore, high temperature (22–35°C), high humidity, abundant inoculum, poor sanitation, dense canopy, and presence of young susceptible tissues are the most favorable conditions for the development of stem canker disease. If sanitation is neglected, disease management becomes difficult with the onset of warmer temperatures and the rainy season. (Salunkhe et al., 2023)
Disease cycle:
The disease cycle of stem canker in dragon fruit caused by the fungus Neoscytalidium dimidiatum:
1. Overwintering and Survival:

The cycle begins with the fungus surviving the off-season as arthroconidia, chlamydospores, and within pycnidia (fruiting bodies) located on previously diseased plant tissue or pruned stems left in the field.
2. Dispersal and Inoculation:

During favorable conditions, primary inoculum (spores) like conidia and pycnidiospores are released. These spores are dispersed to healthy dragon fruit cladodes (stems) via wind, rain splash, or contaminated farming tools.
3. Attachment and Penetration:

Once a spore lands on a susceptible host, it germinates and forms a specialized infection structure called an appressorium. The fungus then enters the host tissue through direct penetration of the cuticle, natural openings like stomata, or physical wounds on the stem.
4. Colonization and Tissue Collapse:

After entering, the fungus establishes itself within the epidermal cells and begins to invade the underlying mesophyll cells. As the hyphae spread, they cause the internal host tissue to break down, leading to the collapse of mesophyll cells and vascular tissue.
5. Host Response and Symptom Development:

The dragon fruit plant attempts to defend itself by forming thickened cell walls and a "walling-off" zone to isolate the infection. This leads to the characteristic elevation of the diseased area, resulting in a raised, crusty scab and sunken stem cankers. In some cases, the plant may exhibit gummosis (oozing sap) as a stress response.
6. Reproduction and Secondary Infection:

Within the mature canker, the fungus produces new pycnidia and arthroconidia. These spores are pushed to the surface of the scab, where they can be dispersed again to cause secondary infections on neighboring stems, continuing the cycle throughout the growing season.

• Regular scouting should be done to detect the disease at an early stage
• Pruning of infected cladodes should be carried out during winter and early spring
• Diseased plant parts must be removed and destroyed to reduce the source of infection
• Maintain proper orchard sanitation by clearing infected debris from the field
• Ensure good air circulation through proper spacing and pruning
• The pathogen destroys plant tissues, causing permanent lesions on fruits and reducing market value by 60–80%
• Fungicides like azoxystrobin and cyprodinil + fludioxonil should be used judiciously (maximum four applications per year)
• Rotate fungicides with different FRAC groups to prevent resistance development

Cactus virus X (CVX) has been extensively studied since it was first described by Amelunxen (1958), who recognized rod-shaped particles in Opuntia monacantha in Germany. CVX is currently classified in the genus Potexvirus, family Alphaflexiviridae, and has a positive-sense single stranded RNA (+) ssRNA) unipartite genome and total genome size of 6.5 kb. The virions of CVX are rod-shaped, filaments are 520 nm long and 13 nm wide (Kim et al., 2016).
Host range:

Cactus virus X has been detected in many cacti plants, including Austrocylindropuntia, Cereus, Echinocereus, Echinopsis, Epiphyllum, Eriocereus, Ferrocactus, Hylocereus, Lobivia, Mammillaria, Notacactus, Opuntia, Pereskia, Platyopuntia, Saguaro, Schlumbergera, and Zygocactus (Park et al., 2018).
Symptoms:

Symptoms of Cactus Virus X (CVX) infection vary widely, making diagnosis difficult, as some infected plants may even appear symptomless. The most common external symptom is systemic mottling, which appears as irregular light and dark green patterns on the plant surface, although this symptom alone is not reliable because other viruses can produce similar effects. In many cases, mottling is accompanied by chlorosis (yellowing) and necrosis (death of tissue). Infected plants may also show reduced growth and overall stunted development, indicating the negative effect of the virus on plant physiology. Morphological abnormalities are also common. These include distorted areoles, deformed spines, twisting of stems, and rough surface growth, especially in cactus species and dragon fruit (Hylocereus spp.). On stems, symptoms may appear as irregular chlorotic spots, halos, or red-brown bordered lesions, which can later turn into necrotic patches or sunken lesions. In severe cases, entire stems may show discoloration or deformation. In dragon fruit, symptoms include mottling, chlorosis, necrotic spots, and reduced vigor, sometimes occurring as secondary infections. Overall, symptom expression depends on the virus strain, host plant, and environmental conditions (Parameswari et al. 2022).
Co-infection of CVX with other cacti viruses:

Cactus Virus X (CVX) is capable of co-infecting plants along with other viruses. Li et al. (2015) reported mixed infections of CVX in Hylocereus undatus with other potexviruses such as zygocactus virus X and pitaya virus X. CVX occurring together with both potexviruses and tobamoviruses in Notocactus leninghausii f. cristatus in Korea, including viruses like cactus mild mottle virus, pitaya virus X, rattail cactus necrosis-associated virus, Schlumbergera virus X, and zygocactus virus X.
Transmission:

The transmission of Cactus Virus X (CVX) primarily occurs through mechanical means. Since no insect or animal vectors have been identified, the virus spreads mainly via activities such as grafting or direct plant-to-plant contact. There is currently no confirmed evidence of seed transmission. However, some studies suggest a possible role of pollen in virus spread. Milbrath and Nelson (1972) observed that symptom development often begins at the onset of flowering, leading to the hypothesis that pollen from infected plants may carry the virus. This indicates that transmission could occur during pollination. Nevertheless, pollen-mediated transmission has not yet been fully verified across different cactus species and requires further investigation.
Management:
• Remove and destroy infected plants completely, as the virus is present in high concentration in plant sap and can easily spread.
• Maintain strict sanitation by disinfecting pruning and grafting tools with bleach or other suitable disinfectants after each use.
• Ensure early detection of infected plants so that they can be removed quickly to prevent further spread in the orchard.
• Avoid using infected stem cuttings for planting, as vegetative propagation is a major source of virus transmission.
• Use seed-derived planting material where possible, since there is no confirmed seed transmission, although this method takes more time.
• Follow good hygiene practices in the field to maintain virus-free planting material and reduce contamination risks.
• Adopt resistant or genetically improved varieties, such as RNAi-based CVX-resistant lines, for long-term management.
• Use transgenic plants with CVX coat protein gene RNAi, which have shown normal growth and resistance compared to non-transgenic infected plants.
• Bacterial soft rot/Watery stem rot (Enterobacter cloacae, Xanthomonas campestris)
Symptoms:

Symptomatic stems at different developmental stages were observed in commercial pitahaya plantations. The disease initially appeared as small, water-soaked yellow spots, which gradually progressed into soft, watery rot surrounded by a yellowish pre-necrotic margin. The infection commonly began at the tips or along the protruding edges of the stems and then advanced toward the center. In some cases, the rot remained confined to specific sectors of the stem, while in others it spread extensively, leading to complete tissue decay. Affected plants exhibited yellowish to brownish, soft, and water-soaked lesions on both stems and fruits. On the stems, the infected tissues became foul-smelling, softened, and eventually rotted, often leaving the main vascular strand intact. In fruits, the rot progressed rapidly, resulting in complete destruction within three days of symptom appearance. When the rot remained localized, the decomposed tissue separated naturally from the healthy portions due to its own weight, leaving the epidermis and vascular tissues still attached to the intact stem. As the remaining epidermis dried, it developed a soft, sometimes crusty, whitish texture that could be easily removed upon handling. (Mizrahi et al., 2002).
Species: Enterobacter cloacae (Jordan 1890) Hormaeche and Edwards 1960

Enterobacter cloacae is a Gram-negative, rod-shaped, facultative anaerobic bacterium belonging to the family Enterobacteriaceae. It is commonly found in soil, water, and plant surfaces, where it usually exists as a harmless saprophyte. However, under favorable environmental conditions or when plants are stressed, it can act as an opportunistic pathogen. At least five members of the family Enterobacteriaceae were successfully infected with plant tissues. These included Enterobacter cloacae, Enterobacter aerogenes (syn. Klebsiella mobilis), Klebsiella oxytoca, Pantoea dispersa, and Rahnella aquatilis. They produced colonies that varied in colour from cream to yellowish, and the bacterial cells ranged in size from approximately 1.9–6.3 × 0.5–2.8 µm. (Masyahit et al., 2009)
Favorable condition:

The disease develops best under warm temperatures ranging from about 30°C to 37°C Nishijima et al. (2004), where the pathogen remains highly active and multiplies rapidly. High relative humidity, especially around 80–90%, creates ideal conditions for infection and rapid disease spread. Excess moisture in the field, particularly under dense planting and poor air circulation, strongly favours disease development. Heavy rainfall during flowering and fruiting stages increases moisture levels and enhances disease incidence. Waterlogged soils and poorly drained fields provide a suitable environment for bacterial infection and survival. Frequent wetting of plant surfaces due to overhead irrigation promotes infection and spread of the pathogen. (Derso et al., 2007).
Infection process:

Enterobacter cloacae causes soft rot in dragon fruit (Hylocereus undatus) by infecting through injuries, producing cell wall-degrading enzymes (pectinase, cellulase), and causing rapid, smelly, watery decay of stem and fruit tissues. The infection can destroy fruit in three days, with symptoms appearing within 24–48 hours post-inoculation.

The infection process begins when the bacterium enters the plant through wounds such as cuts, bruises, or insect bites, as it is unable to penetrate healthy, intact tissues directly. These entry points provide easy access for the pathogen to colonize internal plant tissues. Once inside, the bacterium actively multiplies and produces cell wall–degrading enzymes such as pectinase, polygalacturonase, and cellulase. These enzymes break down the middle lamella and cell walls, resulting in the softening and disintegration of plant tissues, a process known as maceration. As the infection progresses, visible symptoms start to develop. On stems, small yellow, water-soaked spots appear initially, which gradually enlarge and turn into soft, foul-smelling, brown rotting lesions, often leaving the central vascular bundle intact. In fruits, the infection advances rapidly, converting the tissues into a soft, watery pulp that ultimately leads to complete collapse. In the later stages, the bacterium spreads from the initial infection site to surrounding tissues, leading to extensive decay. The affected areas become soft, dark, and necrotic, resulting in severe tissue breakdown and overall plant deterioration.
Management:
Remove infected stems as soon as they are noticed, cutting at least 5–10 cm below the diseased part, and dispose of them away from the field to stop further spread.
• Clean and disinfect pruning tools after each cut using 70% alcohol or 1% bleach solution to avoid transferring the bacteria to healthy plants.
• Do not overwater the crop and ensure proper drainage, as excess moisture and waterlogging encourage disease development.
• Use only healthy and disease-free planting material and allow cuttings to dry in shade for 4–5 days before planting so that wounds can heal properly.
• Spray copper-based bactericides or antibiotics such as streptomycin sulphate or tetracycline hydrochloride (10–100 ppm) to control the bacterial population.
• Apply beneficial bio-control agents to naturally suppress the pathogen in the field.
• Provide balanced fertilizers to keep plants strong and more resistant to infection.
• Regularly check the crop, especially during warm and humid weather, and remove infected parts at an early stage to prevent the disease from spreading.
Reddish brown spot (Nigrospora lacticolonia):

Dragon fruit is a high-value crop that is widely exported and commonly consumed fresh. However, farmers frequently encounter various pests and diseases during its cultivation. In two commercial farms located in Negeri Sembilan and Johor, disease incidence and severity were recorded at approximately 20% and 10%, respectively. In Malaysia, symptoms are typically observed on the stems, whereas in Guangdong Province, infections have been reported on both stems and fruits. If not properly managed, the disease can spread quickly and significantly reduce yields. In Malaysia, Nigrospora species have been linked to several host plants, including Musa species, Catharanthus roseus, and mangrove plants. Similar to other fungal pathogens, Nigrospora can persist on infected plant material, serving as a source of inoculum that facilitates further spread to other plants. Among the diseases affecting dragon fruit, brown spot disease (also known as gecko fungus) is particularly destructive. It can lead to severe crop losses, make fruits unsuitable for export, and increase production costs, ultimately affecting farmers’ productivity and profitability.
Symptoms:

Initial symptoms appear as small, light to dark brown, circular, and slightly sunken spots on the stems or fruits. These spots often develop darker or reddish margins, making them more noticeable against healthy tissue. Under favorable conditions such as high humidity, the lesions enlarge and may merge, forming extensive necrotic patches. As the disease progresses, the infected areas become dry, rough, and corky, sometimes leading to cracking of the stem surface. A yellowish halo may surround the lesions, indicating the spread of infection. In severe cases, large portions of the stem may become blighted, reducing plant vigor and productivity. When fruits are infected, their quality deteriorates, making them unsuitable for consumption or export.
Pathogen

x: Species: Nigrospora lacticolonia Mei Wang & L. Cai (2017)

blocks.x: The disease is caused by Nigrospora lacticolonia. The fungal colony appears floccose and creamy white, with dark greenish-brown patches visible on both the surface and the reverse side. The hyphae are smooth, hyaline, branched, and septate. The conidiogenous cells range from hyaline to pale brown and vary in shape from subglobose to clavate, with hyaline vesicles present between the conidia and the conidiogenous cells. The conidia are smooth, dark brown to black, solitary, aseptate, and globose to ellipsoidal in shape, measuring approximately 10.6–15.3 × 7.7–12.0 µm.
Favorable condition:

The disease commonly develops during the growth stage of young shoots and fruits, particularly in the rainy season or under conditions of frequent fog, high humidity, and limited sunlight. Such environments favor spore germination and infection, especially at relative humidity levels of around 80–85%. The pathogen also thrives in moderate to warm temperatures, with optimal activity between 25°C and 28°C. Infection is more likely when plant tissues are wounded, as damage caused by insects, handling, or environmental stress creates entry points for the fungus. Poor field sanitation, such as leaving plant debris uncleared and failing to prune and destroy infected branches, further contributes to disease persistence. Dense canopy growth due to overcrowding reduces air circulation, creating a humid microclimate that promotes disease development. In addition, unbalanced fertilization particularly excessive nitrogen and insufficient organic matter and micronutrients can weaken plant resistance. Inadequate water management that keeps the field excessively wet, along with the use of contaminated water for irrigation or spraying, also enhances the spread of the disease.
Disease cycle:

Pathogen and Infection: Nigrospora lacticolonia is identified as a fungal pathogen causing reddish-brown, sunken, or necrotic spots on red-fleshed dragon fruit stems, frequently acting as a wound pathogen. Survival: The fungus survives in infected plant debris, soil, and on alternate hosts in the surrounding environment.
Dissemination: Spores are spread by wind currents, rain splash, irrigation water, and the movement of contaminated tools or agricultural equipment.
Infection and Colonization: Spores land on the stem surface and infect through existing injuries or weakened tissue (e.g., pruning wounds or pest damage).
Disease Development: Warm, humid climates, especially during the rainy season, promote rapid sporulation and infection, leading to visible reddish-brown necrotic spots.
Secondary Infection: The fungus produces new spores on the necrotic tissue, leading to secondary infections, increasing the disease severity over time.
Management:
• Remove and destroy infected stems, fruits, and fallen debris to reduce disease spread.
• Regularly prune diseased branches and take them out of the field for destruction.
• Maintain proper plant spacing to avoid overcrowding and reduce humidity buildup.
• Prune plants to create an open canopy that allows good airflow and sunlight penetration.
• Ensure proper drainage by planting on raised beds and avoiding waterlogging.
• Irrigate carefully to avoid excessive moisture on stems and in the field.
• Apply balanced fertilizers along with well-decomposed organic manure enriched with Trichoderma biological control fungus.
• Supplement with micronutrients to improve plant resistance against disease.
• Apply lime periodically to reduce soil acidity and help suppress pathogens.
• Avoid excessive stimulation of off-season flowering to prevent plant stress.
• Maintain overall plant health to improve natural resistance to disease.
• Monitor weather conditions closely, especially during high humidity, cloudy, or rainy periods.
• Start preventive spraying before disease appears or at early stages, especially during favorable conditions.
• Ensure thorough spraying, covering the entire canopy, especially inner and lower parts of the plant.
• Spray Difenoconazole 350 SC or Azoxystrobin + Difenoconazole 320 SC in rotation, 2–3 times at 4– 5 day intervals depending on disease severity and weather.
